summary:
Región del Bío-Bío stands under Chile's statutory framework for trans people, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis, with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees the recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

Facility placement is the region's documented failure. On 14 October 2016 Movilh-Biobío filed a formal complaint with the Seremi de Salud, Mauricio Careaga Lemus, concerning the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where patient Hanna Jiménez Carrasco, interned from 28 September to 3 October 2016, was placed and treated as male despite public policy and the legal duty to use her chosen name and social sex. The complaint alleged brutal and illegal discriminatory acts by hospital staff. The national gender-identity statute, Law 21.120, took effect only in December 2019, after the denunciation. For a visitor, an emergency-room or inpatient admission in Bío-Bío therefore carries a documented precedent of gender-mismatched placement.

Regional incident volume is comparatively high. Movilh's XXIII Annual Human Rights Report, published in March 2025 with 2024 data, records Bío-Bío at 5.89% of the national case total, the third-highest share of any Chilean region, with Concepción among the cities recording the most documented incidents at five.

Violence remains a live risk nationally. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Hostility inside state institutions is also on the record. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.
tangentialFactors:
The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report, published in 2025, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

At regional level, Concepción's municipality dismissed the staff of its Oficina de la Diversidad y No Discriminación during the January 2025 honorary-staff cuts of roughly 100 workers, removing a local point of contact for non-discrimination complaints.

The Bío-Bío figures are a comparison point rather than an outlier of the same order as the capital: five documented incidents in Concepción in 2024 against a national total in which the region held 5.89%, while the two most severe trans-specific assaults on record — the 2023 killing and the September 2021 hotel attack — occurred elsewhere, in the Santiago metropolitan area.
localsOnly:
Residents can change their legal gender on a self-determination basis under Law 21.120, in force since December 2019, with no medical diagnosis, surgery or court order required. Birth certificates allow a third sex marker for intersex children.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry and adopt jointly since March 2022, and to enter civil unions since 2015. Sexual orientation and gender identity function as statutory aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences, a provision in force since 2012.

Trans people held in custody are entitled to recognition of their assumed gender, to housing segmented by gender identity, to gender-appropriate entry examinations and to access by trans visitors, under the protocol signed by the national director of Gendarmería de Chile and monitored by a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives.

The 2016 complaint against the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción was lodged with the Seremi de Salud, the regional health authority, which is the competent channel for a patient placed contrary to their chosen name and social sex. Concepción's municipal diversity and non-discrimination office lost its staff in the January 2025 cuts, reducing local support for residents bringing such complaints.

Isabella Panes's 2025 lawsuit against Carabineros indicates that employment discrimination and exposure of a trans officer's private life remain contested matters inside the national police.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2016 complaint to the Seremi de Salud produced a finding, sanction or remedy is not sourced in this record; the denunciation and its allegations are documented, the outcome is unresolved.

How consistently the Gendarmería protocol is applied in Bío-Bío facilities, and whether any monitoring-committee findings for the region have been published, is not sourced here.

Incident counts for Bío-Bío outside Concepción's five documented cases in 2024, and the national denominator behind the 5.89% share, are not given in the inventory; the share is as published by Movilh.

No source in this record establishes whether Law 21.120 altered inpatient placement practice in the region after 2019, so the 2016 hospital incident is the only documented facility-misassignment data point available.

The current status of Equality and Trans Rights bills before the Chilean Congress, and of the rejected non-discrimination reform, is unresolved in this record beyond the 2024 and 2025 Movilh assessments.
